title: About
text: Home About About the Olympiad Since 2020, the Sustainable Olympiad has brought students together to compete, collaborate and innovate for a healthier planet.

title: Our mission
text: We believe the people who will live longest with the consequences of today's environmental choices deserve the tools, knowledge and platform to shape them. The Sustainable Olympiad is a non-profit, international competition for students aged 12 to 25. Teams investigate an environmental problem in their own community, design a solution, test it and share what they learn, guided by mentors and assessed by experts. Unlike traditional olympiads, success is not only about knowing the right answer. It is about making a measurable difference and inspiring others to follow. “We started with a question about our cafeteria bins. We finished with a product that a local cooperative now makes every week.” Planet Award winning team, 2025

title: Our goals
text: Inspire action Turn concern about the environment into practical, measurable projects. Build skills Develop scientific thinking, creativity, teamwork and communication. Connect communities Link students, schools, researchers and businesses across borders. Include everyone Keep participation free, accessible and open to every school.

title: Our values
text: Evidence over opinion. We value honest data, including results that did not go to plan. Collaboration over competition. Teams compete, but every project and every lesson is shared openly. Access for all. No fees, low-cost materials, travel support and full accessibility. Practise what we teach. Our Finals are low-waste, mostly plant-based and carbon-accounted.

title: Our history
text: From an online experiment during school closures to a global community. 2020 The first Olympiad Three science teachers launch an online challenge for 40 teams from 14 countries during school closures. 2021 Going global A free mentor programme opens, and participation triples to 120 teams. 2022 First in-person Finals Finalists meet in Lisbon, and the University division is introduced. 2023 Open Planet Foundation joins Student grants of up to €5,000 help winning teams turn prototypes into real projects. 2024 Accessibility first Captioned sessions, screen-reader-compatible quizzes and travel support become standard, and the Climate Solutions category is introduced. 2025 Sixth edition A record 280 teams from 62 countries take part; the winning team turns cafeteria waste into bioplastic.

title: Who organises the Olympiad

title: The six categories
text: Every category is open to all three divisions. Briefs are deliberately open, so you can adapt them to your local context.

title: Renewable Energy
text: Design ways to generate, store or save clean energy in your school and community. Teams investigate how communities can move away from fossil fuels. Projects may range from a solar-powered phone charging station to an energy audit that cuts a school's electricity bill. 2026 challenge brief Reduce your school's energy use by at least 15% using low-cost, renewable or efficiency-based measures. Example projects Small-scale solar, wind or micro-hydro prototypes Energy audits and behaviour-change campaigns Low-cost thermal insulation or passive cooling Useful skills Physics, engineering, data analysis Register for this challenge : Renewable Energy

title: Waste Reduction & Circular Economy
text: Rethink how products are made, used and reused so less ends up in landfill. Teams tackle the full life cycle of materials, from reducing single-use plastics to turning food waste into compost, biogas or new products. 2026 challenge brief Cut the waste your school or neighbourhood sends to landfill and show measurable results over one week. Example projects Composting and food-waste recovery systems Repair cafés, swap shops and reuse schemes Biodegradable or upcycled materials Useful skills Chemistry, biology, entrepreneurship Register for this challenge : Waste Reduction & Circular Economy

title: Sustainable Design & Architecture
text: Create products, buildings and public spaces that do more with less. Teams apply eco-design principles to everyday objects, buildings or neighbourhoods, considering materials, energy, water and the wellbeing of the people who use them. 2026 challenge brief Redesign one space or product in your community so that it uses fewer resources and serves people better. Example projects Green roofs, shading and natural ventilation Products designed for repair and disassembly Accessible, low-carbon public spaces Useful skills Design, mathematics, art, technology Register for this challenge : Sustainable Design & Architecture

title: Climate Solutions
text: Measure, communicate and act on climate change, locally and globally. Teams develop tools, campaigns or policy proposals that reduce emissions or help communities adapt to a changing climate, backed by sound data. 2026 challenge brief Calculate a real carbon footprint in your community and propose a credible plan to reduce it. Example projects Carbon calculators and climate data dashboards Flood, heat or drought adaptation plans Climate communication and advocacy campaigns Useful skills Geography, statistics, communication Register for this challenge : Climate Solutions

title: Water & Oceans New
text: Protect fresh water and marine life through smart monitoring and conservation. New for 2026. Teams explore water scarcity, pollution and ocean health, building solutions that save, clean or protect water resources. 2026 challenge brief Monitor a local water source for one month and design an intervention that improves its quality or reduces its use. Example projects Low-cost water quality sensors Rainwater harvesting and grey-water reuse Beach and river clean-up data projects Useful skills Biology, chemistry, electronics Register for this challenge : Water & Oceans

title: Biodiversity & Food Systems
text: Grow food sustainably and give nature space to thrive. Teams work on pollinator habitats, school gardens, urban farming or reducing the footprint of what we eat, combining field observation with practical action. 2026 challenge brief Increase biodiversity on your school grounds and document the change with a species survey. Example projects Pollinator gardens and wildlife corridors Hydroponics and vertical farming Low-impact school menus Useful skills Biology, ecology, nutrition Register for this challenge : Biodiversity & Food Systems

title: Rulebook contents
text: 1. Eligibility 2. Teams and mentors 3. Registration 4. Competition format 5. Project submissions 6. Judging 7. Academic integrity 8. Safety and ethics 9. Code of conduct 10. Accessibility and reasonable adjustments 11. Intellectual property and media 12. Prizes

title: 1. Eligibility
text: The Olympiad is open to students aged 12 to 25 who are enrolled in a school, college or university during 2026. Junior division: students aged 12–14 on 1 August 2026. Senior division: students aged 15–18 on 1 August 2026. University division: undergraduate students aged 18–25. A team competes in the division of its oldest member.

title: 2. Teams and mentors
text: Each team has 2 to 5 students and one supervising mentor aged 21 or over, normally a teacher or lecturer. Students may belong to only one team per edition. A mentor may supervise up to three teams. Mentors guide and support, but the work must be done by the students. Team members can be replaced until the Round 1 start date by contacting the organisers.

title: 3. Registration
text: Registration is free and is completed online by the team captain before the registration deadline. Each team chooses one category when registering. The category can be changed until Round 1 starts. For students under 18, the mentor confirms that parental or guardian consent has been obtained. Schools may register more than one team.

title: 4. Competition format
text: The Olympiad has three stages. Teams that do not advance still receive written feedback and a certificate of participation. Round 1, Online Knowledge Challenge: a 90-minute multiple-choice and short-answer quiz taken together as a team. Round 2, Project Challenge: one week to build and test a solution to the category brief, with a report of up to 3,000 words and a three-minute video. Global Finals: a ten-minute presentation and a ten-minute question-and-answer session with the jury, in person or online.

title: 5. Project submissions
text: Round 2 submissions are uploaded through the participant portal before 23:59 Brasília time on the deadline date. Reports are submitted as PDF and videos as MP4 or a public video link. Videos must include captions, and reports must use headings and alt text for images. All sources, data sets and tools, including AI tools, must be credited. Late submissions are accepted only in documented emergencies.

title: 6. Judging
text: Projects are scored by an independent jury of scientists, educators, engineers and entrepreneurs. Each project is reviewed by at least three judges. Environmental impact: 30% Innovation: 25% Feasibility: 20% Scientific rigour: 15% Communication: 10% Judges declare any conflict of interest and do not score teams from their own institution. The jury's decisions are final.

title: 7. Academic integrity
text: Teams must submit their own original work. Plagiarism, data fabrication or undisclosed outside help leads to disqualification. AI tools may be used for research and editing, provided their use is described in the report. Projects must not have won another international competition before.

title: 8. Safety and ethics
text: Experiments must be carried out safely and under adult supervision where needed. No project may harm people, animals or ecosystems. Research with human participants requires informed consent and must protect their privacy. Mains electricity, hazardous chemicals and power tools may be used only under a mentor's supervision.

title: 9. Code of conduct
text: The Olympiad is an inclusive community. Participants, mentors, judges and volunteers treat each other with respect. Harassment and discrimination of any kind are not tolerated. Concerns can be reported confidentially to the organisers at any time.

title: 10. Accessibility and reasonable adjustments
text: We want everyone to be able to take part. Teams can request adjustments such as extra time, screen-reader-compatible quiz formats, sign language interpretation or step-free venue access. Request adjustments in the registration form or by contacting us at least two weeks before the relevant round.

title: 11. Intellectual property and media
text: Teams keep full ownership of their ideas and projects. By entering, teams allow the organisers to share project summaries, photos and videos to promote the Olympiad, with credit. Teams may opt out of photography at the Finals.

title: 12. Prizes
text: Gold, silver and bronze medals are awarded in each category and division. The Planet Award goes to the best project overall. Winning teams receive grants of up to €5,000 to develop their project further. All finalists receive certificates and mentoring from our partners.

title: Participant guidelines
text: Practical advice for every stage of the competition. Before you register Form a team of 2–5 students with a mix of skills: science, design, writing and presenting. Find a mentor, usually a teacher, who can meet with you regularly. Read the rulebook and choose the category that excites your team most. Preparing for Round 1 Review the sustainability topics in the study guide on our Resources page. Practise with past quizzes and agree how your team will divide questions. Test your internet connection and device the day before. Running your project in Round 2 Start with a clear problem statement and measure your baseline before you change anything. Keep a project log with dates, data, photos and decisions. Involve your community: interview the people affected by the problem. Make your report and video accessible, with headings, alt text and captions. Presenting at the Finals Tell a story: the problem, what you tried, what you measured and what you learned. Show real evidence. Judges value honest results, including failures. Rehearse answering questions and share speaking time across the team.

title: Sustainability tips
text: Small everyday actions for students, schools and families. Energy Switch off lights, screens and chargers when you leave a room. Use daylight where you can and choose LED bulbs. Lower the heating by 1 °C. It can cut heating energy use by up to 10%. Waste Carry a reusable bottle, cup and lunch box. Repair, swap or donate before you throw away. Sort your recycling correctly. A contaminated bin can end up in landfill. Water Take shorter showers and turn the tap off while brushing your teeth. Collect rainwater for plants. Report leaking taps and pipes at school. Food Plan meals and use leftovers to reduce food waste. Eat more seasonal, local and plant-based food. Compost fruit and vegetable scraps. Transport Walk, cycle, scoot or take public transport where you can. Share rides for longer journeys. Choose video calls when travelling is not necessary. Nature Plant native flowers for pollinators. Leave a wild corner in gardens and school grounds. Join or organise a local clean-up.

title: General
text: What is the Sustainable Olympiad? An international competition where student teams develop real solutions to environmental challenges in six categories, from renewable energy to biodiversity. Learn more about us . Who can take part? Students aged 12 to 25 who are enrolled in a school, college or university. Teams compete in the Junior (12–14), Senior (15–18) or University (18–25) division. Does it cost anything to participate? No. Registration, all competition rounds and the starter resources are free. Travel support is available for in-person finalist teams. Is the competition held in English? Yes, the Olympiad is run in English. Teams may use translation tools and should mention this in their report. Judges assess ideas, not language skills.

title: Registration
text: How do I register a team? The team captain completes the online registration form before 9 October 2026. You will need the details of every team member and your mentor. Can I take part on my own? Teams need at least two students. If you cannot find teammates, contact us and we will try to match you with other students from your region. Can we change our category or team members after registering? Yes. Changes are allowed until Round 1 starts on 10 October 2026. Email us with your team name and the change. Does our mentor have to be a teacher? Usually yes, but any responsible adult aged 21 or over with a connection to your school or university can act as mentor.

title: Competition
text: Do we need to travel to compete? No. Rounds 1 and 2 take place online from your school. The Global Finals are hybrid, so finalists can present in São Paulo, Brazil, or online. What equipment do we need? A computer with an internet connection is enough for Round 1. For Round 2, most projects use low-cost or recycled materials. Expensive equipment does not earn extra points. Can we use AI tools? Yes, for research and editing, as long as you describe how you used them in your report. The ideas and the work must be your team's own. Are past papers available? Yes. Round 1 papers from previous editions, with mark schemes and worked solutions, are on the Past Papers page. You can practise online or download PDFs. How are projects judged? By an independent jury using five weighted criteria: impact, innovation, feasibility, scientific rigour and communication. See the judging criteria .

title: Support & Accessibility
text: What accessibility support is available? We offer extra time, screen-reader-compatible quizzes, captioned sessions, sign language interpretation and step-free venues. Request adjustments when you register or contact us . How can my school become a partner or host an event? We would love to hear from you. Visit Partners or get in touch . How do you use our personal data? We use registration data only to run the competition, and we never sell it. Mentors confirm guardian consent for participants under 18. Data is deleted 12 months after each edition. Still have a question? Our team usually replies within two working days. Contact us

title: Our commitment
text: This website is designed to conform to the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1 at level AA. Accessibility is part of how we design, write and test every page.

title: Accessibility features
text: A “Skip to main content” link and clear page landmarks for screen readers. Full keyboard support, with a clearly visible focus indicator. title: Question A1 2 marks
text: A rooftop solar module has an area of 1.6 m 2 and an efficiency of 20%. On a day equivalent to 4.5 peak sun hours at 1000 W m −2 , approximately how much electrical energy does it produce? Answer options for question A1 A A: 0.32 kWh B B: 1.44 kWh C C: 7.2 kWh D D: 14.4 kWh Check answer to question A1 Worked solution for question A1 Answer: B. Power at peak irradiance: P = 1.6 m 2 × 0.20 × 1000 W m −2 = 320 W. Energy: 320 W × 4.5 h = 1440 Wh = 1.44 kWh . Option A forgets the 4.5 hours.

title: Question A2 2 marks
text: Over 20 years, the global warming potential (GWP) of methane is about 81, but over 100 years it is only about 28. What is the main reason for this difference? Answer options for question A2 A A: Methane absorbs infrared radiation more strongly as its concentration rises B B: Methane has an atmospheric lifetime of only about 12 years, so most of its warming happens in the first decades C C: Methane is oxidised to CO 2 , which has a higher GWP than methane D D: The 100-year GWP includes absorption of methane by the oceans Check answer to question A2 Worked solution for question A2 Answer: B. GWP compares the warming caused by a pulse of gas with the same mass of CO 2 over a chosen time horizon. Methane is removed (mainly by OH radicals) with a lifetime of about 12 years. Averaged over 100 years, its short, intense effect is diluted, while long-lived CO 2 keeps warming. Option C is false: the CO 2 produced has a GWP of 1 by definition.

title: Question A3 2 marks
text: According to Betz's law, what is the maximum fraction of the kinetic energy flux of the wind that an ideal turbine can extract? Answer options for question A3 A A: 1/3 B B: 1/2 C C: 16/27 D D: 8/9 Check answer to question A3 Worked solution for question A3 Answer: C. Extracting all the energy would stop the air behind the rotor, so no more air could flow through. Momentum theory gives an optimum when the wind is slowed to one third of its upstream speed, giving a maximum power coefficient of 16/27 ≈ 59.3% .

title: Question A4 2 marks
text: The power available to a wind turbine is P = ½ρ Av 3 . If the mean wind speed at a site is 9.0 m s −1 instead of 6.0 m s −1 , by what factor does the available power increase? Answer options for question A4 A A: 1.5 B B: 2.25 C C: 3.375 D D: 4.5 Check answer to question A4 Worked solution for question A4 Answer: C. P ∝ v 3 , so the factor is (9.0/6.0) 3 = 1.5 3 = 3.375 . This is why turbines are placed on hilltops and offshore.

title: Question A5 2 marks
text: The average pH of the surface ocean has fallen from about 8.2 to 8.1 since pre-industrial times. By approximately what percentage has the hydrogen-ion concentration increased? Answer options for question A5 A A: 1% B B: 10% C C: 26% D D: 100% Check answer to question A5 Worked solution for question A5 Answer: C. pH = −log 10 [H + ], so [H + ] new /[H + ] old = 10 8.2 − 8.1 = 10 0.1 ≈ 1.26, an increase of about 26% .

title: Question A6 2 marks
text: Producers in a grassland fix 50 000 kJ m −2 yr −1 . Assuming 10% of the energy is transferred between successive trophic levels, how much energy is available to tertiary consumers? Answer options for question A6 A A: 5000 kJ m −2 yr −1 B B: 500 kJ m −2 yr −1 C C: 50 kJ m −2 yr −1 D D: 5 kJ m −2 yr −1 Check answer to question A6 Worked solution for question A6 Answer: C. Producers 50 000 → primary consumers 5000 → secondary consumers 500 → tertiary consumers 50 kJ m −2 yr −1 . Tertiary consumers are three transfers away from the producers.

title: Question A7 2 marks
text: In a eutrophic lake, which process is most directly responsible for the sharp fall in dissolved oxygen after an algal bloom? Answer options for question A7 A A: Algae absorbing oxygen through their cell walls during the day B B: Aerobic decomposition of dead algae by bacteria C C: Nitrogen fixation by cyanobacteria D D: An increase in oxygen solubility as the water cools Check answer to question A7 Worked solution for question A7 Answer: B. When the bloom dies, the huge mass of organic matter is broken down by aerobic bacteria, whose respiration consumes dissolved oxygen faster than it can be replaced. During the day algae photosynthesise and release oxygen, and cooler water holds more oxygen, so A and D are wrong.

title: Question A8 2 marks
text: Which of the following is a negative (stabilising) feedback in the climate system? Answer options for question A8 A A: The ice–albedo feedback B B: Release of methane from thawing permafrost C C: The water-vapour feedback D D: Increased emission of infrared radiation from a warmer surface Check answer to question A8 Worked solution for question A8 Answer: D. By the Stefan–Boltzmann law, a warmer surface emits more radiation (∝ T 4 ), which opposes further warming. This is the Planck response. The other three amplify an initial warming, so they are positive feedbacks.

title: Question A9 2 marks
text: A geothermal power plant takes heat from a reservoir at 180 °C and rejects heat to cooling water at 30 °C. What is its maximum theoretical (Carnot) efficiency? Answer options for question A9 A A: 17% B B: 33% C C: 67% D D: 83% Check answer to question A9 Worked solution for question A9 Answer: B. Temperatures must be in kelvin: η = 1 − T C / T H = 1 − 303.15/453.15 = 0.331 ≈ 33% . Options A and D come from wrongly using degrees Celsius.

title: Question A10 2 marks
text: A heat pump with a coefficient of performance (COP) of 3.5 delivers 14 kW of heat to a building. At what rate does it extract heat from the outside air? Answer options for question A10 A A: 3.5 kW B B: 4.0 kW C C: 10 kW D D: 49 kW Check answer to question A10 Worked solution for question A10 Answer: C. Electrical input = 14 kW / 3.5 = 4.0 kW. By conservation of energy, heat delivered = heat extracted + work input, so heat extracted = 14 − 4.0 = 10 kW .

title: Question A1 2 marks
text: A classroom replaces a 60 W filament bulb with an 8 W LED bulb that gives the same light. The light is on for 5 hours a day, 365 days a year. How much energy is saved in a year? Answer options for question A1 A A: 9.5 kWh B B: 94.9 kWh C C: 109.5 kWh D D: 949 kWh Check answer to question A1 Worked solution for question A1 Answer: B. Power saved = 60 − 8 = 52 W. Energy = 52 W × 5 h × 365 = 94 900 Wh = 94.9 kWh . Option C is the total energy used by the old bulb, not the saving.

title: Question A2 2 marks
text: Which energy source does NOT originally come from sunlight? Answer options for question A2 A A: Wind B B: Hydroelectric C C: Wood D D: Tidal Check answer to question A2 Worked solution for question A2 Answer: D. The Sun heats the air unevenly (wind), evaporates water that later flows downhill (hydro) and powers photosynthesis (wood). Tides are caused mainly by the Moon's gravity acting on a rotating Earth.

title: Question A3 2 marks
text: In photosynthesis, 6CO 2 + 6H 2 O → C 6 H 12 O 6 + 6O 2 . How many molecules of oxygen are released for each molecule of glucose made? Answer options for question A3 A A: 1 B B: 3 C C: 6 D D: 12 Check answer to question A3 Worked solution for question A3 Answer: C. The balanced equation shows 6 O 2 molecules for every one glucose molecule.

title: Question A4 2 marks
text: In the food chain grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → hawk, the grass stores 100 000 kJ of energy. If 10% of the energy passes from each level to the next, how much reaches the hawk? Answer options for question A4 A A: 1000 kJ B B: 100 kJ C C: 10 kJ D D: 1 kJ Check answer to question A4 Worked solution for question A4 Answer: C. 100 000 → 10 000 (grasshopper) → 1000 (frog) → 100 (snake) → 10 kJ (hawk). There are four transfers, not five.

title: Question A5 2 marks
text: Making a can from recycled aluminium instead of from bauxite ore saves about how much of the energy? Answer options for question A5 A A: About 10% B B: About 40% C C: About 70% D D: About 95% Check answer to question A5 Worked solution for question A5 Answer: D. Extracting aluminium from its ore needs huge amounts of electricity for electrolysis. Melting down scrap needs only about 5% of that, saving about 95% .

title: Question A6 2 marks
text: Which greenhouse gas is the most abundant in Earth's atmosphere? Answer options for question A6 A A: Carbon dioxide B B: Methane C C: Water vapour D D: Ozone Check answer to question A6 Worked solution for question A6 Answer: C. Water vapour is the most abundant greenhouse gas. Its amount is controlled by temperature, so it amplifies warming caused by CO 2 rather than starting it.

title: Question A7 2 marks
text: Seawater has a density of about 1.025 g cm −3 . Which plastic will float in the sea? Answer options for question A7 A A: PET, a drinks bottle (1.38 g cm −3 ) B B: PVC, a pipe (1.38 g cm −3 ) C C: Polypropylene, a bottle cap (0.90 g cm −3 ) D D: Solid polystyrene, a CD case (1.05 g cm −3 ) Check answer to question A7 Worked solution for question A7 Answer: C. Only materials less dense than seawater float: polypropylene (0.90 < 1.025). This is why bottle caps are often found on beaches while the bottles sink, unless air is trapped inside.

title: Question A8 2 marks
text: A flight emits 0.15 kg CO 2 per passenger per km. Lisbon to Paris is 1450 km. How much CO 2 is emitted for one passenger making a return trip? Answer options for question A8 A A: 43.5 kg B B: 217.5 kg C C: 435 kg D D: 4350 kg Check answer to question A8 Worked solution for question A8 Answer: C. Return distance = 2 × 1450 = 2900 km. 2900 × 0.15 = 435 kg . Option B is a one-way trip.

title: Question A9 2 marks
text: Two meadows each contain 100 plants of the same 4 species. Meadow X has 25 of each species. Meadow Y has 97 of one species and 1 of each of the others. Which statement is correct? Answer options for question A9 A A: Both have the same biodiversity because they have the same number of species B B: Meadow X has higher biodiversity because the species are more evenly spread C C: Meadow Y has higher biodiversity because one species is very successful D D: Biodiversity cannot be compared without knowing the area Check answer to question A9 Worked solution for question A9 Answer: B. Biodiversity depends on richness (number of species) and evenness (how equally they are represented). Richness is equal, but X is far more even , so it is more diverse.

title: Question A10 2 marks
text: Why do tropical rainforest soils often become poor for farming only a few years after the forest is cleared? Answer options for question A10 A A: Tropical soils contain too much nitrogen B B: Most nutrients are stored in the living plants, and heavy rain washes the rest out of the thin soil C C: The soil becomes too cold without the trees D D: Earthworms eat all the organic matter Check answer to question A10 Worked solution for question A10 Answer: B. In rainforests, nutrients are recycled quickly and held mainly in the vegetation. Once the trees are removed, heavy rainfall leaches the few remaining nutrients from the thin topsoil.

title: Part A: Multiple choice 20 marks
text: Each question is worth 2 marks. Choose one answer.

title: Question A1 2 marks
text: A home battery stores 13.5 kWh and has a round-trip efficiency of 90%. How much energy must be supplied while charging so that it can deliver 13.5 kWh? Answer options for question A1 A A: 12.2 kWh B B: 13.5 kWh C C: 15.0 kWh D D: 24.3 kWh Check answer to question A1 Worked solution for question A1 Answer: C. Energy in × 0.90 = 13.5 kWh, so energy in = 13.5 / 0.90 = 15.0 kWh . Option A wrongly multiplies by 0.90.

title: Question A2 2 marks
text: The band gap of crystalline silicon is 1.12 eV. What is the longest wavelength of light that can create an electron–hole pair in silicon? Answer options for question A2 A A: 443 nm B B: 700 nm C C: 1110 nm D D: 1550 nm Check answer to question A2 Worked solution for question A2 Answer: C. λ = hc / E = (6.63 × 10 −34 × 3.00 × 10 8 ) / (1.12 × 1.60 × 10 −19 ) = 1.11 × 10 −6 m = 1110 nm , in the near infrared. Longer wavelengths pass straight through.

title: Question A3 2 marks
text: What is the approximate maximum efficiency of a single-junction solar cell under ordinary sunlight (the Shockley–Queisser limit)? Answer options for question A3 A A: 15% B B: 33% C C: 59% D D: 86% Check answer to question A3 Worked solution for question A3 Answer: B. Photons below the band gap are not absorbed, and the excess energy of high-energy photons is lost as heat. Together these limit a single junction to about 33% . 86% is the limit for an infinite stack of junctions under concentrated light.

title: Question A4 2 marks
text: Which organisms fix atmospheric nitrogen in the root nodules of legumes such as beans and clover? Answer options for question A4 A A: Nitrifying bacteria such as Nitrosomonas B B: Denitrifying bacteria such as Pseudomonas C C: Rhizobium bacteria D D: Mycorrhizal fungi Check answer to question A4 Worked solution for question A4 Answer: C. Rhizobium lives symbiotically in root nodules and converts N 2 into ammonium using the enzyme nitrogenase. Nitrifying bacteria oxidise ammonium to nitrate, and denitrifiers return nitrogen to the air.

title: Question A5 2 marks
text: A river sample has a high biochemical oxygen demand (BOD). This most likely indicates: Answer options for question A5 A A: a high concentration of dissolved oxygen B B: a large amount of biodegradable organic matter, for example from sewage C C: a low concentration of nitrate D D: a high salinity Check answer to question A5 Worked solution for question A5 Answer: B. BOD measures the oxygen that microorganisms consume while decomposing organic matter (usually over 5 days at 20 °C). A high BOD means a lot of organic pollution , which will lower dissolved oxygen.

title: Question A6 2 marks
text: A pumped-storage reservoir holds 1.0 × 10 6 m 3 of water at an average height of 300 m above the turbines. How much gravitational potential energy is stored? Answer options for question A6 A A: 8.2 MWh B B: 82 MWh C C: 818 MWh D D: 8.2 GWh Check answer to question A6 Worked solution for question A6 Answer: C. m = 1.0 × 10 9 kg. E = mgh = 1.0 × 10 9 × 9.81 × 300 = 2.94 × 10 12 J. Dividing by 3.6 × 10 9 J per MWh gives 818 MWh .

title: Question A7 2 marks
text: Global demand for a resource grows at 7% per year. Approximately how long does it take for demand to double? Answer options for question A7 A A: 7 years B B: 10 years C C: 14 years D D: 70 years Check answer to question A7 Worked solution for question A7 Answer: B. Doubling time = ln 2 / ln 1.07 = 10.2 years. This matches the 'rule of 70': 70/7 = 10 years .

title: Question A8 2 marks
text: Taking Earth's albedo as 0.30 and ignoring the atmosphere, what is Earth's effective radiating temperature? Answer options for question A8 A A: About −18 °C B B: About 0 °C C C: About +15 °C D D: About +33 °C Check answer to question A8 Worked solution for question A8 Answer: A. Absorbed = emitted: S (1 − α)/4 = σ T 4 , so T = (1361 × 0.70 / (4 × 5.67 × 10 −8 )) 1/4 = 255 K ≈ −18 °C . The actual average of +15 °C is 33 K warmer because of the natural greenhouse effect.

title: Question A9 2 marks
text: How much energy is needed to heat 150 L of water from 15 °C to 55 °C? Answer options for question A9 A A: 0.70 kWh B B: 6.97 kWh C C: 25.1 kWh D D: 69.7 kWh Check answer to question A9 Worked solution for question A9 Answer: B. Q = mc Δ T = 150 × 4.18 × 40 = 25 080 kJ. Dividing by 3600 kJ per kWh gives 6.97 kWh . Option C is the answer in MJ, not kWh.

title: Question A10 2 marks
text: What is meant by 'green hydrogen'? Answer options for question A10 A A: Hydrogen made from natural gas, with the CO 2 captured and stored B B: Hydrogen made by electrolysis of water using renewable electricity C C: Hydrogen made by gasifying coal D D: Hydrogen made by steam reforming of methane without carbon capture Check answer to question A10 Worked solution for question A10 Answer: B. Green hydrogen comes from electrolysis powered by renewables. A is 'blue', C is 'brown/black' and D is 'grey' hydrogen, which is how most hydrogen is made today.

title: Question B1: Reusable or single-use? 9 marks
text: Manufacturing a reusable glass bottle causes 0.40 kg CO 2 e. Each use cycle (collection, washing and refilling) adds 0.03 kg CO 2 e. A single-use aluminium can causes 0.17 kg CO 2 e per use, including recycling. (a) Part a: Find the minimum number of uses for the bottle's footprint per use to be lower than the can's. 3 marks Worked solution for question B1 part a Need (0.40 + 0.03 n )/ n < 0.17, so 0.40 < 0.14 n and n > 2.86. The bottle must be used at least 3 times . Marking: 1 mark for the inequality; 1 mark for solving it; 1 mark for rounding up to a whole number. (b) Part b: Calculate the footprint per use if a bottle is used 20 times, and the percentage saving compared with the can. 2 marks Worked solution for question B1 part b (0.40 + 20 × 0.03)/20 = 1.00/20 = 0.050 kg per use. Saving = (0.17 − 0.050)/0.17 = 71% . Marking: 1 mark each. (c) Part c: In reality, after each use a bottle is returned with probability p = 0.90, otherwise it is lost. Show that the expected number of uses is 1/(1 − p ), and calculate the expected footprint per use. 4 marks Worked solution for question B1 part c A bottle is used exactly k times with probability p k −1 (1 − p ). So E[ k ] = Σ k p k −1

title: Question B2: A solar farm 8 marks
text: A solar farm has a peak capacity of 50 MW and a capacity factor of 18%. An average household uses 3500 kWh of electricity per year. Electricity from coal emits 0.95 kg CO 2 per kWh. (a) Part a: Calculate the farm's annual electricity output, in GWh. 2 marks Worked solution for question B2 part a 50 MW × 8760 h × 0.18 = 78 840 MWh = 78.8 GWh . Marking: 1 mark for the method; 1 mark for the answer. (b) Part b: How many average households could this supply? 2 marks Worked solution for question B2 part b 78 840 000 kWh / 3500 kWh = about 22 500 households . Marking: Allow error carried forward. (c) Part c: How much CO 2 per year is avoided if this output replaces coal-fired electricity? 2 marks Worked solution for question B2 part c 78 840 000 × 0.95 = 7.49 × 10 7 kg ≈ 74 900 t of CO 2 . Marking: Allow error carried forward. (d) Part d: Give two reasons why the capacity factor of a solar farm is far below 100%. 2 marks Worked solution for question B2 part d Any two of: no output at night; clouds; low sun angle in winter and in the early morning and evening; panels lose efficiency when hot; dust and soiling; inverter and cable losses. Marking: 1 mark each.

title: Question B3: Sewage effluent in a river 8 marks
text: Upstream of a treatment plant, a river flows at 4.0 m 3 s −1 with a BOD of 2.0 mg L −1 and dissolved oxygen (DO) of 9.0 mg L −1 . The plant discharges 0.50 m 3 s −1 of effluent with a BOD of 60 mg L −1 and DO of 2.0 mg L −1 . Assume complete mixing. (a) Part a: Calculate the BOD of the river just below the outlet. 2 marks Worked solution for question B3 part a BOD = (4.0 × 2.0 + 0.50 × 60)/(4.0 + 0.50) = 38/4.5 = 8.4 mg L −1 . Marking: 1 mark for the flow-weighted mean; 1 mark for the answer. (b) Part b: Calculate the dissolved oxygen just below the outlet. 2 marks Worked solution for question B3 part b DO = (4.0 × 9.0 + 0.50 × 2.0)/4.5 = 37/4.5 = 8.2 mg L −1 . Marking: 1 mark for the method; 1 mark for the answer. (c) Part c: Ignoring re-aeration, would the DO stay above 5.0 mg L −1 (needed by most fish) once all the BOD has been exerted? Explain. 2 marks Worked solution for question B3 part c The oxygen demand (8.4) exceeds the oxygen available (8.2), so DO would fall to zero : the river would become anoxic and fish would die. Marking: 1 mark for comparing the values; 1 mark for the conclusion. (d) Part d: What is the maximum effluent BOD that would keep the DO at or above 5.0 mg

title: Question B4: Fertilisers and nitrous oxide 8 marks
text: Ammonium nitrate (NH 4 NO 3 ) and urea (CO(NH 2 ) 2 ) are common nitrogen fertilisers. (a) Part a: Calculate the percentage by mass of nitrogen in each fertiliser. 2 marks Worked solution for question B4 part a NH 4 NO 3 : 28.02/80.05 = 35.0% . Urea: 28.02/60.06 = 46.7% . Marking: 1 mark each. (b) Part b: A farmer applies 120 kg of nitrogen per hectare to 15 ha using urea. What mass of urea is needed? 2 marks Worked solution for question B4 part b N needed = 120 × 15 = 1800 kg. Urea = 1800/0.4665 = 3858 kg ≈ 3.86 t . Marking: 1 mark for total N; 1 mark for the answer. (c) Part c: 1.0% of the applied nitrogen is emitted as nitrogen in N 2 O. Calculate the mass of N 2 O and its CO 2 -equivalent. 3 marks Worked solution for question B4 part c N 2 O–N = 18 kg. title: Question B5: How long will it last? 7 marks
text: Known reserves of a metal are 880 Mt, and current annual consumption is 26 Mt. (a) Part a: Calculate the static lifetime of the reserves. 1 mark Worked solution for question B5 part a 880/26 = 34 years (33.8). Marking: 1 mark. (b) Part b: If consumption grows continuously at 3.0% per year, cumulative use after t years is ( C 0 / r )(e rt − 1). Calculate when the reserves run out. 4 marks Worked solution for question B5 part b 880 = (26/0.030)(e 0.030 t − 1), so e 0.030 t = 1 + 0.030 × 880/26 = 2.015. Then t = ln(2.015)/0.030 = 23 years . Steady 3% growth cuts the lifetime by a third. Marking: 1 mark for setting up the equation; 1 mark for rearranging; 1 mark for the logarithm; 1 mark for the answer. (c) Part c: Give two reasons why the real lifetime could be longer than either estimate. 2 marks Worked solution for question B5 part c Any two of: higher prices make lower-grade deposits economic, so reserves grow; new discoveries; recycling; substitution by other materials; more efficient use. Marking: 1 mark each. End of paper. Try another past paper .

title: Question A1 2 marks
text: A 2000 W kettle is switched on for 3 minutes. How much energy does it use? Answer options for question A1 A A: 0.01 kWh B B: 0.1 kWh C C: 6 kWh D D: 360 kWh Check answer to question A1 Worked solution for question A1 Answer: B. 3 minutes = 0.05 h. Energy = 2.0 kW × 0.05 h = 0.1 kWh (360 000 J).

title: Question A2 2 marks
text: In which layer of the atmosphere is most of the ozone layer found? Answer options for question A2 A A: Troposphere B B: Stratosphere C C: Mesosphere D D: Thermosphere Check answer to question A2 Worked solution for question A2 Answer: B. About 90% of atmospheric ozone is in the stratosphere , roughly 15–35 km up, where it absorbs harmful UV radiation.

title: Question A3 2 marks
text: Which of these crops does NOT depend on insects for pollination? Answer options for question A3 A A: Apple B B: Almond C C: Wheat D D: Strawberry Check answer to question A3 Worked solution for question A3 Answer: C. Wheat , like other grasses, is wind-pollinated (and mostly self-pollinating). Apples, almonds and strawberries need insects such as bees.

title: Question A4 2 marks
text: A plant has plenty of water in its soil. What happens to its rate of transpiration on a hot, dry, windy day? Answer options for question A4 A A: It decreases, because wind closes the stomata B B: It increases, because water vapour diffuses away from the leaves faster C C: It stays the same D D: It stops completely Check answer to question A4 Worked solution for question A4 Answer: B. Heat, dry air and wind all steepen the water-vapour gradient between the leaf and the air, so transpiration increases . Stomata close only when the plant is short of water.

title: Question A5 2 marks
text: Last year a town produced 600 t of waste and recycled 30% of it. This year the waste fell by 10% and the recycling rate rose to 40%. How much more waste was recycled this year? Answer options for question A5 A A: 18 t B B: 36 t C C: 54 t D D: 60 t Check answer to question A5 Worked solution for question A5 Answer: B. Last year: 0.30 × 600 = 180 t. This year: waste = 540 t, recycled = 0.40 × 540 = 216 t. Difference = 36 t .

title: Question A6 2 marks
text: Making one cotton T-shirt uses about 2700 L of water. A class of 30 students each buys 2 fewer T-shirts this year. How much water is saved? Answer options for question A6 A A: 5400 L B B: 81 000 L C C: 162 000 L D D: 1 620 000 L Check answer to question A6 Worked solution for question A6 Answer: C. 30 × 2 × 2700 = 162 000 L , about the volume of a small swimming pool.

title: Question A7 2 marks
text: What causes coral bleaching? Answer options for question A7 A A: Corals expel the algae living in their tissues when the water becomes too warm B B: Strong sunlight bleaches the coral's pigment C C: Chlorine pollution from swimming pools D D: Fish eat the colourful algae on the reef Check answer to question A7 Worked solution for question A7 Answer: A. Corals depend on algae called zooxanthellae for food and colour. Heat stress makes the corals expel the algae , leaving the white skeleton visible. The coral may starve if it lasts too long.

title: Question A8 2 marks
text: Which item takes the longest to break down in the sea? Answer options for question A8 A A: Paper bag B B: Aluminium can C C: Plastic bottle D D: Glass bottle Check answer to question A8 Worked solution for question A8 Answer: D. Estimates: paper, weeks; aluminium can, about 200 years; plastic bottle, about 450 years; glass , up to a million years. Glass is inert, so it is far less harmful than plastic.

title: Question A9 2 marks
text: On a 1:50 000 map, a forest is a rectangle 3 cm by 2 cm. What is its real area? Answer options for question A9 A A: 6 ha B B: 15 ha C C: 150 ha D D: 1500 ha Check answer to question A9 Worked solution for question A9 Answer: C. 3 cm = 1.5 km and 2 cm = 1.0 km. Area = 1.5 km 2 = 150 ha . Do not scale the area by 50 000; the area scale is 50 000 2 .

title: Question A10 2 marks
text: Which shows the energy transfers in a hydroelectric power station? Answer options for question A10 A A: Gravitational potential → kinetic → electrical B B: Chemical → thermal → electrical C C: Kinetic → gravitational potential → electrical D D: Thermal → kinetic → electrical Check answer to question A10 Worked solution for question A10 Answer: A. Water stored high up has gravitational potential energy, which becomes kinetic energy as it falls, turning the turbine and generator to produce electrical energy.

title: Question B1: A shorter shower 8 marks
text: Leo takes an 8-minute shower every day with a shower head that uses 12 L per minute. He switches to a 5-minute shower with an eco shower head that uses 8 L per minute. The water is heated from 15 °C to 40 °C. (a) Part a: How much water does Leo save each day? 2 marks Worked solution for question B1 part a Before: 8 × 12 = 96 L. After: 5 × 8 = 40 L. Saving = 56 L . Marking: 1 mark for both volumes; 1 mark for the saving. (b) Part b: How much water does he save in a year? 2 marks Worked solution for question B1 part b 56 × 365 = 20 440 L . Marking: Allow error carried forward. (c) Part c: Calculate the energy saved in a year by not heating this water, in kWh. 4 marks Worked solution for question B1 part c Mass = 20 440 kg. Energy = 20 440 × 4.18 × 25 = 2 135 980 kJ. Dividing by 3600 kJ per kWh gives 593 kWh . Marking: 1 mark for the mass; 1 mark for ΔT = 25 °C; 1 mark for kJ; 1 mark for converting to kWh.

title: Question B2: Can trees cancel our emissions? 7 marks
text: A growing tree absorbs on average 22 kg of CO 2 per year. A family's car and heating emit 7.5 t of CO 2 per year. A forest has about 400 trees per hectare. (a) Part a: How many trees are needed to absorb the family's emissions? 2 marks Worked solution for question B2 part a 7500 kg / 22 kg = 340.9, so 341 trees (always round up). Marking: 1 mark for converting tonnes to kg; 1 mark for the answer. (b) Part b: What area of forest is this, in hectares? 2 marks Worked solution for question B2 part b 341 / 400 = 0.85 ha (8500 m 2 ), larger than a football pitch. Marking: Allow error carried forward. (c) Part c: Give two reasons why planting trees alone is not a solution to climate change. 3 marks Worked solution for question B2 part c Any two well-explained points: young trees absorb very little for many years; the carbon is released again if the trees burn, die or are cut down; there is not enough land to offset everyone's emissions; cutting emissions is faster and permanent. Marking: Up to 2 marks per reason (maximum 3).

title: Question B3: Counting daisies 7 marks
text: A field measures 50 m by 40 m. Students place ten 1 m 2 quadrats at random and count the daisies in each: 4, 7, 3, 0, 6, 5, 8, 2, 5, 10. (a) Part a: Calculate the area of the field. 1 mark Worked solution for question B3 part a 50 × 40 = 2000 m 2 . Marking: 1 mark. (b) Part b: Calculate the mean number of daisies per m 2 . 2 marks Worked solution for question B3 part b Total = 50 daisies in 10 m 2 , so the mean is 5.0 per m 2 . Marking: 1 mark for the total; 1 mark for the mean. (c) Part c: Estimate the total number of daisies in the field. 2 marks Worked solution for question B3 part c 5.0 × 2000 = 10 000 daisies . Marking: Allow error carried forward. (d) Part d: Why should the quadrats be placed at random, and why is it better to use more quadrats? 2 marks Worked solution for question B3 part d Random placement avoids bias, such as choosing spots with lots of daisies. More quadrats give a more reliable mean because daisies are not evenly spread. Marking: 1 mark each.

title: Question B4: Electric or petrol? 8 marks
text: An electric car uses 16 kWh per 100 km. Electricity costs €0.22 per kWh and causes 0.25 kg CO 2 per kWh. A petrol car uses 6.0 L per 100 km. Petrol costs €1.80 per litre, and burning 1 L releases 2.3 kg CO 2 . (a) Part a: Calculate the fuel cost per 100 km for each car. 2 marks Worked solution for question B4 part a Electric: 16 × 0.22 = €3.52 . Petrol: 6.0 × 1.80 = €10.80 . Marking: 1 mark each. (b) Part b: Calculate the CO 2 per 100 km for each car. 2 marks Worked solution for question B4 part b Electric: 16 × 0.25 = 4.0 kg . Petrol: 6.0 × 2.3 = 13.8 kg . Marking: 1 mark each. (c) Part c: A family drives 12 000 km a year. How much money would they save on fuel with the electric car? 2 marks Worked solution for question B4 part c 12 000 km = 120 × 100 km.
